sections.name: Combat System Engineering — FPS & TPS
sections.explanation_simple: Combat systems are the heart of action games. When you press the fire button in Call of Duty or swing a sword in Dark Souls, a chain of systems kicks in: the game checks if you hit something, calculates how much damage to do, checks if the enemy has any special defenses, plays a hit animation, subtracts health, and shows damage numbers. The difference between a good combat system and a great one is 'juice' - how satisfying every action feels through screen shake, sound effects, particle effects, and controller vibration.
key_concepts: Hitscan: Instant hit detection (bullet travels instantly - used in most shooters)
Projectile: Actual object flies through the air (rockets, grenades, arrows)
Raycast: A line is cast from camera/barrel to check what it hits
Damage Over Time (DoT): Poison/fire that deals damage gradually
Area of Effect (AoE): Damage in a radius (explosions)
Hitbox: The area on a character that can be hit (exact shape matters hugely)
Hurtbox: Area where damage is applied (can be different from visual mesh)
IFrames: Invincibility frames during rolls/dodges (Dark Souls classic)
Stun Lock: Being unable to act because you keep getting hit
Hitstun: Momentary pause when hit (feeds the feeling of impact)
Combo: Chain of attacks that flow into each other
Canceling: Cutting one animation short by starting another (advanced technique)

sections.name: Technical Art & VFX Pipelines
sections.explanation_simple: Technical Art is the bridge between artists and programmers. A Technical Artist (TA) takes beautiful art and makes it work in the game engine efficiently. They create shaders that make water look real, set up particle systems for explosions, optimize 3D models so they run fast, and build tools that help artists work faster. If game programming is building the engine, and game art is designing the car, technical art is making sure the car actually runs and looks great doing it.
key_concepts: Shader Graph: Visual shader creation (Unity Shader Graph, Unreal Material Editor)
Niagara: Unreal Engine's next-gen VFX system (replaces Cascade)
VFX Graph: Unity's VFX system for GPU-powered particles
Material Instancing: One master material, many instances with different settings
Texture Baking: Converting 3D detail into 2D textures (normal maps, AO maps)
UV Optimization: Arranging UV islands efficiently to maximize texel density
LOD (Level of Detail): Creating lower-poly versions for distance rendering
Houdini Engine: Running Houdini inside the game engine for procedural assets
Shader Permutations: Avoiding too many shader variants (kills performance)
Render Passes: Separating scene elements for post-processing compositing

code_examples.title: Unreal Niagara VFX: Explosion System
code_examples.code:
// Niagara Explosion Effect - Blueprint-like pseudocode for visual setup
/*

NIAGARA EMITTER: Explosion_Core
  - Emitter Update:
    - Set Lifespan: 2.0 seconds
    - Spawn Burst: 500 particles
  - Particle Spawn:
    - Initialize Particle Position: Sphere Location (Radius=5)
    - Initialize Particle Velocity: Random (Speed=200-500, Direction=Outward)
    - Initialize Particle Color: Orange-Yellow gradient
    - Initialize Particle Size: Random (5-15)
  - Particle Update:
    - Scale Color Over Life: Yellow -> Orange -> Red -> Transparent
    - Scale Size Over Life: 1.0 -> 3.0 -> 0.0
    - Drag: 0.8 (slow down over time)
    - Add Velocity Noise: Turbulence effect
  - Render:
    - Sprite Renderer with "fire_particle" texture
    - Blend Mode: Additive (glow effect)

NIAGARA EMITTER: Explosion_Shockwave
  - Emitter Update:
    - Set Lifespan: 0.5 seconds
    - Spawn Burst: 1 (single ring)
  - Particle Spawn:
    - Initialize Particle Position: 0
    - Initialize Particle Size: 0.5
  - Particle Update:
    - Scale Size Over Life: 0 -> 100 (ring expands)
    - Scale Color Over Life: White -> Transparent
  - Render:
    - Ribbon Renderer (ring shape)
    - Blend Mode: Additive

NIAGARA EMITTER: Explosion_Debris
  - Emitter Update:
    - Set Lifespan: 3.0 seconds
    - Spawn Burst: 30 particles
  - Particle Spawn:
    - Initialize Mesh: Random debris meshes (rocks, metal chunks)
    - Initialize Velocity: Outward with upward bias
    - Initialize Angular Velocity: Random spin
  - Particle Update:
    - Apply Gravity
    - Apply Air Resistance
    - Bounce on collision with ground
  - Render:
    - Mesh Renderer
    - Casts shadows
*/

// To spawn from C++:
void AMyCharacter::SpawnExplosion(FVector Location)
{
    if (ExplosionEffect)
    {
        UNiagaraComponent* NiagaraComp = UNiagaraFunctionLibrary::SpawnSystemAtLocation(
            GetWorld(),
            ExplosionEffect,
            Location,
            FRotator::ZeroRotator,
            FVector(1.0f),
            true,  // Auto destroy
            true,  // Auto activate
            ENCPoolMethod::AutoRelease
        );

        if (NiagaraComp)
        {
            NiagaraComp->SetNiagaraVariableFloat("ExplosionRadius", ExplosionRadius);
            NiagaraComp->SetNiagaraVariableColor("ExplosionColor", FLinearColor::MakeRandomColor());
        }
    }
}

sections.name: Cinematics & Story Systems
sections.explanation_simple: Cinematics in games are like making a movie inside the game engine. You control cameras, characters, lighting, and sound to tell a story. In AAA games, this means full motion capture (actors performing scenes), carefully framed camera shots from multiple angles, lip-synced dialogue, and sometimes even virtual production (using LED walls like The Mandalorian). For smaller games, you can still do effective storytelling with dialogue systems, branching conversations, and carefully placed cameras.
key_concepts: Sequencer (Unreal): Timeline-based cinematic editor like Premiere Pro inside UE
Timeline (Unity): Similar timeline-based animation and event system
Camera Cuts: Switching between camera angles (wide, medium, close-up)
Dolly: Camera moving along a track (smooth movement)
Crane Shot: Camera moving up or down
Dutch Angle: Tilted camera for unease/disorientation
Depth of Field: Blurring background to focus on subject
Cross Dissolve: Smooth transition between shots
Motion Capture: Recording actor performances for realistic animation
Lip Sync: Matching mouth movements to dialogue audio
Dialogue Trees: Branching conversation systems (massive spreadsheets)
Subtitle Systems: Displaying dialogue text with speaker names
QTEs (Quick Time Events): Button prompts during cutscenes

sections.name: Game UI/UX Design & Implementation
sections.explanation_simple: Game UI is everything the player sees and interacts with outside of the game world: health bars, ammo counters, inventory screens, pause menus, settings, and HUD elements. Great game UI is invisible - you don't think about it, you just use it naturally. Bad game UI makes you frustrated because you can't find what you need. Diegetic UI is when the UI exists inside the game world itself (like the health bar on Dead Space's suit, or the map in Far Cry that's literally a GPS device your character holds).
key_concepts: Diegetic UI: UI that exists in the game world (character's watch, car dashboard)
Non-Diegetic UI: Traditional HUD elements floating on screen
Spatial UI: UI positioned in 3D space (health bar above enemy heads)
Meta UI: Menus, inventory, settings outside gameplay
HUD: Heads-Up Display (health, ammo, minimap - always visible)
UX Flow: How the player moves through screens (main menu -> options -> game)
Controller Navigation: D-pad movement between UI elements
Focus Groups: Elements that "pop" when selected
Accessibility: Color blindness options, subtitle sizing, control remapping
Responsive UI: UI that works at different resolutions and aspect ratios
